definition: Rule-based machine translation (RBMT) is a classical approach of machine translation systems based on linguistic information about source and target languages.
details: Such information is retrieved from (unilingual, bilingual or multilingual) dictionaries and grammars covering the main semantic, morphological, and syntactic regularities of each language. Having input sentences, an RBMT system generates output sentences on the basis of analysis of both the source and the target languages involved. RBMT has been progressively superseded by more efficient methods, particularly neural machine translation.

explainer.lead: Rule-based machine translation builds translations from linguistic knowledge of the source and target languages, drawn from dictionaries and grammars. It matters as the classical MT approach that neural methods have largely superseded.

tiers.eli5: The system uses grammar books and dictionaries to take a sentence apart in one language and rebuild it in another, like a very literal translator.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers rely on it where linguistic rules can be curated and outputs must be predictable, or as a baseline. A pitfall is that rule coverage is costly to build and brittle on irregular or informal language.
tiers.paperLevel: Systems analyse the input sentence using unilingual, bilingual, or multilingual dictionaries and grammars covering semantic, morphological, and syntactic regularities, then generate the output sentence from that analysis; quality is bounded by the coverage of the hand-built resources.

explainer.example: A dictionary maps each source word to target equivalents and grammar rules reorder them per target syntax, producing a translation without any learned model.
